transcript:
# Day 16, Philosophy: Zeno's paradoxes and Democritus's atoms (Zeno of Elea, c. 490 to 430 BC; Democritus, c. 460 to 370 BC)

Picture a runner on a track. Before she can reach the finish line, she has to get halfway there. Before she reaches the halfway point, she has to get a quarter of the way. Before that, an eighth. And so on, forever. There are infinitely many steps to complete before she arrives, and nobody can finish an infinite list of tasks. So she never starts. Yet you just watched her cross the line. Something in the argument is broken, and figuring out what took the smartest people in the world more than two thousand years.

That is Zeno of Elea, a student of Parmenides. Last time you met Parmenides, who argued that change and motion are illusions. Zeno's job was to defend the boss. His move was clever: instead of arguing that motion is impossible, he assumed motion is real and showed it leads to absurd results. If believing in motion gets you into contradictions, maybe Parmenides was right all along. He wrote something like forty of these arguments. The best known are the Dichotomy (the runner above), Achilles and the Tortoise (a fast runner can never catch a slow one with a head start, because every time he reaches where the tortoise was, it has moved a bit further), and the Arrow (at any single instant, a flying arrow occupies a space exactly its own size, so it is at rest; if it is at rest at every instant, it never moves).

The word for this kind of argument is a paradox: a chain of reasoning where every step looks fine but the conclusion is clearly false. Paradoxes are useful because they tell you one of your assumptions is wrong, even when you cannot yet see which one.

Democritus went in the opposite direction from Zeno. Rather than denying change, he asked what the world would have to be made of for change to work. His answer: tiny, indivisible, unchanging particles moving through empty space. He called them atoms, from the Greek word for uncuttable. Everything you see, from a horse to a hurricane, is atoms rearranging. Nothing is truly created or destroyed. Change is real, but it is just the shuffling of permanent pieces. This solves Parmenides's puzzle (how can something come from nothing?) by saying it never does. The pieces were always there.

Notice what Democritus did. He kept the one thing Parmenides was sure about, that reality has an unchanging core, and moved it down a level, from the whole universe to the smallest parts. That is a classic strategic move: concede the strongest point and reframe where it applies.

Now the objections. Zeno's paradoxes are usually said to have been "solved" by calculus in the 1600s, since the infinite series one half plus one quarter plus one eighth adds up to exactly one. The runner's infinite steps take a finite total time. Many philosophers find this unsatisfying. The math shows the total is finite, but it does not explain how you complete infinitely many separate acts. That debate, under the name supertasks, is still live. The Arrow paradox is handled differently: modern physics defines velocity at an instant as a limit, so being "frozen" at an instant is not the same as being at rest.

Democritus looks like a prophet, but be careful. His atoms were a philosophical guess, not an experimental result, and the actual atoms discovered in the 1800s turned out to be cuttable after all. His real insight was the method: explain the visible by the invisible, and explain change by rearrangement. That idea runs through all of modern science. His critics, Aristotle chief among them, argued that empty space was impossible and that purely mechanical atoms could not account for purpose or quality. Aristotle won that argument for almost two thousand years.

You can see the thread from the Milesians, who wanted natural explanations, through Heraclitus and Parmenides, who split on whether anything stays put, to Zeno and Democritus, who each took a side and pushed it as far as it would go. There is also a link to Game Theory and Decisions: Zeno's method of assuming your opponent's position and deriving absurdity is exactly how you test a strategy before committing to it.

Question for the day: when something in your work looks impossible on paper but clearly happens in practice, which assumption in the paper version is wrong?

Primary source: Aristotle's Physics, Book 6, Chapter 9, where he lays out and answers Zeno's four motion paradoxes. For Democritus, the surviving fragments are collected in any edition of the Presocratic philosophers; look for the line about sweetness and color existing by convention while only atoms and void exist in truth.
